newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW-German import prices, Hesse CPI.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-German import prices, Hesse CPI.

text.p: The following are comments made by economists on German inflation data released this morning. German January import prices rose 1.0 percent from December and were up 2.6 percent year-on-year. February consumer price data for the state of Hesse showed a rise of 0.3 percent month-on-month and a 1.5 percent increase year-on-year.

UWE ANGENENDT, BHF-BANK: "Import prices were of course driven by the strong dollar and raw materials. For February consumer prices we have to expect fairly high month-on-month rates but that is due to seasonal factors like higher food and energy prices. I expect the other states will show even higher month-on-month CPI growth rates than Hesse. I don't think consumer inflation will this year fall back to the levels seen in 1996 but I don't expect an acceleration in inflation. Inflation is not going to be a problem, real wage increases are too low for that."

ARMIN KAYSER, SWISS BANK CORP : "The rise in import prices was not unexpected given the depreciation of the mark, but it is surprising that the mark fall had such a rapid effect on import prices. I expect import prices rises will reach four or five percent year-on-year in the coming months. But the domestic inflation trend remains weak due to low wage increases, which are keeping service prices low. Rents are also likely to remain stable over the coming months. The chances are good that consumer price inflation won't climb over two percent in the coming months. But we may get close to two percent by the end of the year. The Hesse figures were a touch lower than expected. the market expects month-on-month inflation of 0.4 percent."

LOTHAR HESSLER, TRINKAUS & BURKHARDT: "Import prices were stronger than expected. The oil price and the dollar are having an effect. For this year, import price inflation will remain clearly above consumer price inflation, and that is a negative factor. But it is too early to conclude that the Bundesbank's medium-term inflation goal of 1.5 to 2.0 percent for this year is in danger. On the positive side, rents are not rising and real wage increases remain weak so, that is giving some compensation." --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
